title: What Does It Mean for My Team to Win Today
author: Admired Leadership
summary: The post borrows from athletics, where competitors know at once whether they won, to argue that workplaces lack the same clarity. When team members know what winning looks like each day, they engage more and learn faster. The author proposes that leaders have every team member name a highest priority for the day and report at day's end whether they achieved it. Posting these wins publicly builds interest in one another's work and a rhythm of daily success. The author stresses the practice is easy despite sounding laborious, and closes by asking whether your team knows what winning today means.
points: Competitors get a clear win or loss answer, but most workplaces never define what winning means day to day.
Having each person name a top priority gives every role a daily, achievable win.
Asking people to post whether they hit that priority is effectively asking whether they won.
Sharing priorities with peers increases engagement and mutual interest.
quotes: The same idea applies to the workplace. When team members know what it means to win every day, they become more engaged and committed. Everyone enjoys winning, so they prepare and practice with vigor. Their ability to learn and improve goes up dramatically, as well.

The problem is that what it means to win every day in the workplace isn’t always clear. In fact, for many team members, what counts as winning lacks any clarity at all. Leaders can design scorecards so that every team member understands what it means to win. That produces an animated team with a commitment toward daily success.
But nothing beats the satisfaction of completing the highest priority of the day.
Leaders who expect team members to articulate their highest priority of the day promote a focus on winning.
Just knowing what team members believe is their highest priority and having people share this with each other creates more engagement and interest.
